notes:
I've arranged these notes verse by verse. I used Enduring Word (Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, the commentaries collected on Bible Hub and StudyLight (Gill, Ellicott, Barnes, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Keil & Delitzsch, Cambridge Bible, Coffman, Chuck Smith, Constable), Spurgeon, Augustine (on New Advent), Bible.org, GotQuestions and GTY.

**What I couldn't find:**
- Clear disagreements on this psalm between Protestant traditions (Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican), stated by each tradition's own teachers.
- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm.
- NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or anything on catholic.com or oca.org.

I also couldn't read the end of Enduring Word's page (my copy stopped at v. 15). So I've left those topics out, and v. 20 is thin.

---

**Title / vv. 1–2**
- The title calls it both a "Song" and a "Psalm." It is the first psalm since Psalm 50 that isn't credited to David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Guzik quotes Cresswell (via Spurgeon): the Greek church said this psalm on Easter Day, and the Greek Bible calls it "A Psalm of the Resurrection." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- "All the earth": the psalm has the whole world in view, not just Israel. God is God over everyone, so everyone is called to praise him joyfully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: the whole world is invited to share Israel's joy. "Make His praise glorious" means praising God for his greatness and majesty, not just thanking him for personal kindness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): the title points to Christ and the resurrection. "Every land" means not Judea alone but the universal Church spread through the world. He takes "jubilate" as wordless rejoicing, joy too great to put into words. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801066.htm

**v. 3**
- "Say to God": the psalmist gives practical words for praise. Spoken praise should not be neglected. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- The enemies' "submission": several commentators, including Spurgeon and Maclaren, read this as forced or pretended homage. Power brings a person to their knees, but only love wins the heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit agrees: God's enemies are made to submit against their will, so the submission is pretended. His rescues are "terrible" to persecutors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Augustine: why should God's works be feared rather than loved? Because God works in us by grace, so believers rejoice "with trembling." Gentile Christians should not look down on the Jews or on heretics who have been "cut off." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801066.htm

**v. 4**
- "Your name" stands for God's character. This praise knows something of who God is, and goes beyond the grudging submission of v. 3. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit cites Dr Kay: Psalms 65–68 clearly have "the universality of the Church" in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 5**
- Calvin: the verse quietly rebukes people's common thoughtlessness about God's works. "Come and see" implies the works are there for anyone to see. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-5.html
- Spurgeon: the parting of the Red Sea is a standing wonder that still calls out "Come and see." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps066.cfm
- Pulpit: to save his people, God has to strike their enemies; that is the sense in which he is "awesome" (terrible). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Gill reads the verse about Christ: his miracles, his preaching, the righteousness he worked out for his people, and his finished work of redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-5.htm
- Dating the psalm: Clarke compares the return from Babylon with the Exodus. Coffman suggests the nations were invited to look at Sennacherib's dead army. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-5.html

**v. 6**
- The verse recalls two crossings: the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan (Joshua 3). Both show God taking an active part in human affairs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- "There we rejoiced": by saying "we," the psalmist counts himself among Israel centuries earlier. Spurgeon adds that Israel's joy was in God himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: the crossing was all joy for Israel but terrible for the Egyptians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the church points the world to the Exodus wonders, because what it has seen in its own day shows God's power is unchanged. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-5.htm

**v. 7**
- God keeps watch over the nations, so rebelling or exalting yourself against him is foolish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: God watches the hostile nations so his people come to no harm. Their outward submission can't be trusted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Augustine: if our own strength lasted forever, we would never have fallen. We are strong only by sharing in God's power. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801066.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- Kidner (cited by Guzik): Israel's fortunes take in the whole world. God keeps his people alive and keeps them standing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: vv. 8–15 are "the heart of the psalm," praise for a recent rescue from a long oppression. Verse 9 means God "has set" our soul in life, which implies there had been great danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Augustine: "the voice of his praise" is the confession that whatever good we are, we are by his grace. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801066.htm

**v. 10**
- God's blessing sometimes comes as testing. Guzik uses the picture of a refiner skimming off the dross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: refining silver the old way took a long time, so the image suggests Israel's suffering lasted a long time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Gill: in trials God tests and refines his people's faith, patience, hope and love. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-10.html
- Augustine: God refined us like silver, not like hay. His fire washed off our impurity instead of burning us to ashes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801066.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik takes "net" and "burdens" as pictures of lost freedom and heavy pressure. Kidner says the word for "affliction" occurs nowhere else; it may come from a root meaning "to press." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit rejects Cheyne's rendering "dungeon," because the word always means "net" or "stronghold." The sense is being crushed under heavy oppression. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 12**
- "Ride over our heads": Pulpit compares Egyptian and Assyrian carvings of kings driving chariots over fallen enemies. "Fire and water" is a proverbial phrase for every kind of danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Poole: oppressors used Israel "like slaves, yea, like beasts." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- The word for "abundance" means "abundant drink." It appears only here and in Psalm 23:5 ("runneth over"). Ellicott prefers the Greek and Latin rendering "refreshment," or with a small change, "a broad place." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-12.htm
- Guzik: the affliction was in some sense "from You." The rich fulfilment would never have come without the hardship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Gill applies the verse to the Church: the burning of the martyrs, and a well-watered, spiritually plentiful "latter day." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-12.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) reads it spiritually: "abundance in Christ," the riches of God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-12.html
- Coffman takes it fairly literally: wealth recovered after Sennacherib's army died. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-12.html
- Henry: affliction can make even the poorest place a wealthy place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-12.html

**vv. 13–14**
- A burnt offering stood for complete dedication (Boice). Failing to keep vows to God damages character (Morgan). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Pulpit: a vow was like a contract with God, and the Mosaic Law allowed several kinds. Vows were usually made in times of trouble (Jephthah, Hannah). The speaker was probably the nation's leader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: "fatlings" are fattened animals. "Incense of rams" means the smoke or pleasing smell of the offering. "Offer" literally means to prepare or dress for sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 16**
- Sacrifice alone didn't fulfil the vow. The psalmist also had to tell what God had done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-66/
- Spurgeon: first they were told to "come and see," now to "come and hear," because "Hearing is faith's seeing." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps066.cfm
- Pulpit: the audience is the godly within Israel. Citing Hengstenberg, it calls vv. 16–20 a teaching passage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit's alternative reading is "praise was under my tongue." The psalmist was so sure of an answer that praise was already on his lips as he prayed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm

**v. 18** (the verse most discussed)
- Barnes: it doesn't mean noticing any sin in yourself, since everyone sees sin in their heart. It means cherishing sin or refusing to give it up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm
- Ellicott: it means having evil deliberately in view; you cannot be forgiven while keeping hold of the sin. He thinks this community claim of innocence points to a late date. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm
- Geneva Bible note: if I delight in wickedness God won't hear, but if I confess it he will receive me. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: a hypocritical prayer is not heard. The answer in v. 19 proves the psalmist's heart was sincere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm
- Matthew Henry: vv. 18–19 work like a logical argument. He rejects a Jewish reading that sins kept in the heart don't count. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-18.html
- Constable (Dallas Seminary, dispensational): God knows all prayers, so he "hears" in that sense, but he won't answer the prayer of someone nursing sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-18.html
- Chuck Smith adds a caution: God does hear sinners who cry for mercy, or no one would be saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/66-18.html
- Bible.org: if God answered only people with no unconfessed sin at all, no prayers would be answered. The issue is wilfully continuing in sin. https://bible.org/question/it-true-it-one-has-unconfessed-sin-their-life-god-does-not-answer-ones-prayers
- GotQuestions calls unconfessed sin the most obvious hindrance to prayer. https://www.gotquestions.org/prayer-hindrances.html
- GTY (John MacArthur) lists this verse among signs of an unbeliever, and concludes God generally does not answer unbelievers' prayers. https://www.gty.org/library/questions/QA160/does-god-answer-the-prayers-of-unbelievers

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: the answer came so clearly that the psalmist couldn't doubt it. It is remarkable that God pays attention to a mere man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
- Cambridge Bible: this is not self-righteousness but a clear conscience; the answer clears him of hypocrisy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm

**v. 20**
- Keil & Delitzsch: prayer and mercy belong together "of call and echo." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/66-18.htm
- Pulpit: the psalm fittingly ends with the psalmist's own blessing of God for special mercy to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/66.htm
